questions.stem: You are examining Roger, 45, in ED. His abdomen is distended. Standing on his right, you percuss from the umbilicus out to the left flank and find dullness in the flank. What is the correct next step to show shifting dullness?
options: Roll him onto his left side, then re-percuss the same spot straight away
Keep a finger on the dull spot, roll him onto his right side, wait, then re-percuss
Have him press a hand along the midline, tap one flank, and feel for a thrill
Sit him upright and percuss down from the costal margin for a fluid level
questions.why: Mark where the dullness starts, roll the patient towards you so that flank is uppermost, wait about 30 seconds for the fluid to move, then percuss again. If ascites is present, the spot that was dull is now resonant.
notes: Lying on the left side keeps the fluid in the left flank, so the spot stays dull and the test cannot show anything; you also need to wait for the fluid to move.
This is the fluid thrill test. It is a different and less sensitive sign that is usually positive only with large, tense ascites, so it is not the next step in shifting dullness.
Sitting him up and looking for a fluid level is not a recognised bedside test for ascites, and it does not show fluid moving with a change in position.

questions.stem: Roger, 45, weighs about 73 kg. His ascitic neutrophil count is 1295 x10^6/L and his creatinine has risen from 72 to 118 µmol/L. IV antibiotics are running in ED. Apart from the antibiotics, which treatment most reduces his risk of hepatorenal syndrome and death?
options: 20% albumin IV, 8 g for every litre of ascites drained at paracentesis
Terlipressin 1 mg IV 6-hourly with 20% albumin 20 to 40 g daily
20% albumin 1.5 g/kg IV within 6 hours, then 1 g/kg IV on day 3
Oral spironolactone 100 mg and furosemide 40 mg daily
questions.why: In SBP, IV albumin 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours of diagnosis and 1 g/kg on day 3, given with antibiotics, lowers the rates of hepatorenal syndrome and death. For Roger the first dose is about 110 g.
notes: This is the albumin dose given to prevent circulatory dysfunction after large-volume paracentesis. It is not the regimen for SBP, and Roger had only a 40 mL diagnostic tap.
Terlipressin with albumin treats established hepatorenal syndrome-AKI once other causes are excluded. It is not the first-line preventive treatment in SBP and needs specialist input.
Diuretics should be withheld in SBP with AKI and falling blood pressure, because they reduce renal perfusion further and can bring on hepatorenal syndrome.

questions.stem: Roger, 45, has SBP on a background of decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis. His systolic BP is falling and his creatinine has risen from 72 to 118 µmol/L. He is given IV albumin to prevent hepatorenal syndrome. Which mechanism is the albumin mainly countering?
options: Splanchnic vasodilatation lowers effective arterial volume, causing renal vasoconstriction
Bacteria from the ascites seed the kidneys and cause acute tubular necrosis
Tense ascites raises intra-abdominal pressure and compresses the renal arteries
Raised bilirubin forms bile casts that block the renal tubules
questions.why: Infection makes the splanchnic vasodilatation of portal hypertension worse, so effective arterial blood volume falls. RAAS, the sympathetic system and ADH are activated, the renal arteries constrict and GFR falls. Albumin expands the circulating volume and has anti-inflammatory effects.
notes: Hepatorenal syndrome is a functional, haemodynamic renal failure. The tubules are structurally normal and the kidneys are not infected.
Very tense ascites can impair renal venous outflow, but this is not the mechanism of hepatorenal syndrome in SBP, and albumin would not relieve compression.
Bile cast nephropathy happens at much higher bilirubin levels, usually above about 340 µmol/L. Roger's is 86, and albumin does not prevent cast formation.

questions.stem: Roger, 45, has cirrhosis with ascites. The ED registrar does a diagnostic tap under ultrasound in the left iliac fossa, about 3 cm superomedial to the anterior superior iliac spine and lateral to the rectus sheath. Which artery is this site mainly chosen to avoid?
questions.why: The inferior epigastric artery runs upward deep to the rectus abdominis, inside the rectus sheath. Putting the needle lateral to the rectus sheath avoids it. Damaging it can cause a large abdominal wall haematoma, especially when platelets are low and the INR is high, as in Roger.
notes: The external iliac artery lies deep in the pelvis and passes under the inguinal ligament. It is well below and away from a correctly placed iliac fossa paracentesis needle.
This small superficial branch runs in subcutaneous tissue towards the ASIS. It is not the vessel the landmark is chosen to avoid.
This artery runs deep along the inguinal ligament and the iliac crest. The paracentesis landmark is defined by staying lateral to the rectus, which protects the inferior epigastric artery.
